analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover mental health and addiction treatment on the same terms as other medical care.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan mental health parity bill with 114 cosponsors died in House committees in the 106th Congress without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred group and individual health plans from putting stricter copayments, visit limits, and dollar caps on mental health and substance abuse treatment than they put on other medical care. It built on a 1996 law that only limited annual and lifetime spending caps, extending parity to day-to-day cost-sharing and treatment limits and closing loopholes in that law. The bill never received a hearing vote, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental illness or addiction, and their families, who would get mental health and substance abuse treatment covered with the same copays, visit limits, and annual and lifetime caps as any other illness. Plan members generally also gain because catastrophic mental health costs would no longer drain annual and lifetime benefit pools.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with mental illness or addiction

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group and individual health plans from imposing treatment limitations or financial requirements on mental health benefits if similar limits are not imposed on medical and surgical benefits [S2][S3].
Extends the same parity rule to substance abuse and chemical dependency benefits, which the 1996 parity law had left out [S3].
Closes the 1996 law's cost exemption and removes its sunset clause, and expands definitions to cover copayments, deductibles, out-of-network charges, annual limits, and lifetime limits [S3].
Applies the requirement to individual-market insurance as well as employer plans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, health insurers and employers sponsoring plans would have borne higher premiums as mental health and addiction coverage was equalized; costs would partly flow to workers through premiums. Employers would still be free to drop mental health coverage entirely, since the bill does not require any plan to offer it.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require any plan to offer mental health or substance abuse benefits at all; a plan can stay compliant by dropping the benefit entirely [S3].

Plans may keep separate reimbursement rates, service delivery systems, and managed-care controls like prior authorization for mental health care, so equal cost-sharing does not guarantee equal access in practice [S3].
Equalizing coverage raises premiums; the 1996 law's exemption for plans whose costs rose 1% or more was removed, so employers with concentrated mental health costs would face the full increase [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core gain — ending higher copays, tighter visit limits, and discriminatory lifetime caps for mental illness and addiction — is substantial for the roughly one in five Americans affected by mental health conditions and for families facing addiction, and it would have applied to both job-based and individual insurance. The bill's real weaknesses are that plans can avoid it by dropping the benefit, that it leaves managed-care controls in place, and that premium increases would flow partly back to workers. On balance it is a genuine consumer protection with significant but not prohibitive cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to their health subcommittees in April and May 1999, and no committee ever acted on it before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Marge Roukema (R-NJ) introduced the bill on April 21, 1999, with an initial bipartisan group of cosponsors including Democrats and Republicans [S3].
It was referred to the Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means Committees, splitting jurisdiction across three committees [S5].

Within weeks it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health, the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations [S5].

The bill reached 114 cosponsors — 95 Democrats, 18 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but no committee or subcommittee scheduled any markup or vote, and no action was taken after the May 1999 subcommittee referrals [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that would have faced higher premiums under broad parity are better off because the bill never advanced. Congress did pass narrower parity extensions in the period, but people with mental illness and addiction kept unequal coverage in the meantime.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers spared higher premiums

for.name: Marge Roukema
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of 22 original cosponsors spanning both parties [S3].

for.name: 18 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members of the moderate Republican wing [S4].

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with primary jurisdiction over health insurance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and sent it to its Health and Health and Environment Subcommittees, where no markup or vote was ever scheduled [S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the portions within their jurisdiction; the bill sat until the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.role: Insurers and employer coalitions opposing broad parity mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed expanding the 1996 parity law to all treatment limits and financial requirements, arguing it would sharply raise premiums; opposition campaigns like these were widely reported during the 1999-2000 parity debate.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan: 95 of 211 House Democrats, 18 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent cosponsored, with a Republican leading the bill; the bill died for lack of committee action, not a partisan vote.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care companies
industries.note: Parity would have ended higher copays, visit limits, and caps on mental health and addiction care, raising insurer costs; the industry's cost argument was the public's lost coverage. The bill did leave managed-care tools like prior authorization intact [S3].

Broader parity would have raised group premiums, though the bill preserved the option to drop mental health benefits to avoid the requirement and delayed compliance for plans under existing collective bargaining agreements [S3].

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: Equal cost-sharing and visit limits would expand the number of patients able to afford therapy, inpatient, and addiction treatment.
